$comment: Rule catalog — leakage. Standards 6, 7, 8, 9. Information reaching the model that will not exist at prediction time. This is the category where the gap between what matters and what is checkable is widest: one entry carries a heuristic detector, and the rest are attestation-only because leakage lives in the semantics of a column rather than in its text.

rules.title: Preprocessing sees only what prediction-time code will see
rules.description: Transformations must be fitted within the training portion of each split, not across data the model should not have seen. Standard 8 P1 and P2 are two source statements of this one prohibition: the general form, and the specific case of fitting scalers, encoders, or imputation globally before a split.
rules.rationale: A scaler fitted on the whole dataset carries the test set's distribution into training. The resulting estimate is optimistic, the model is fine in evaluation and worse in production, and nothing in the output signals which of the two is happening.
rules.remediation: Move preprocessing inside a pipeline that is fitted per split or per fold, so the transformation sees exactly what the inference path will see.
rules.evidenceExpected: Pipeline-scoped preprocessing, or an attestation that every fitted transformation was checked to be fitted on training data only.
rules.$assuranceNote: The check compares in-file ordering: a preprocessing fit appearing before a split call in the same file. Order-in-file is a proxy for order-in-dataflow, and the variable being fit may already be a training subset loaded from disk, so a finding is evidence and not proof. A clean report means only that this pattern was not observed in single-file flows; multi-file pipelines and notebooks executed out of order are not proven clean.

rules.title: Nothing unavailable at prediction time reaches training
rules.description: A model must not be trained on information that will not exist at the moment it makes a prediction. This covers features derived from later events, aggregates computed over windows that include the prediction period, and any join that reaches forward in time.
rules.rationale: A model with access to the future performs beautifully in evaluation and is worthless in production, because the input that carried its performance is not there. Nothing about the evaluation reveals this — the score is high, which is the outcome everyone was hoping for.
rules.remediation: Recompute every feature as of the prediction moment, bound aggregate windows to end before it, and re-evaluate. A model trained on future information cannot be repaired by adjusting its threshold.
rules.evidenceExpected: An attestation from a reviewer who traced each feature's population time against the prediction moment, naming the lineage record and pipeline code examined.
rules.$assuranceNote: Nothing automated establishes this. Whether information was available at prediction time lives in data values and join semantics, not in code text. Flagging date-column usage was considered and rejected as guessing dressed as analysis.
rules.$exemptibilityNote: Non-exemptible. A model trained on the future is invalid rather than non-compliant, and waiving the rule does not make it work — an exception would approve deploying something known not to function as evaluated.

rules.title: The target never enters the features
rules.description: No feature may contain, encode, or be derived from the thing being predicted. This includes fields populated only after the outcome is known, identifiers assigned by the process being predicted, and aggregates computed over a window that includes the label.
rules.rationale: Target leakage is the most damaging failure in this domain and the hardest to see: the feature usually looks legitimate, and the relationship to the target is semantic rather than syntactic. The model is not learning to predict — it is learning to read the answer.
rules.remediation: Remove the feature, or reconstruct it from data available before the outcome. Then re-evaluate: the previous result described a different problem.
rules.evidenceExpected: An attestation from someone who understands the data, confirming per feature that it is not derived from the target or from the process that generates it, and naming the lineage record consulted.
rules.$assuranceNote: Nothing automated establishes this. Detecting target leakage from feature names or correlations was considered and rejected: name similarity fails in both directions constantly, a strong correlation is what a good feature looks like, and a passing result would imply no target leakage — a claim no static scan can make.
rules.$exemptibilityNote: Non-exemptible. A model reading its own answer is invalid rather than non-compliant; an exception would waive the rule while leaving the model unable to do the thing it was evaluated as doing.

rules.title: Feature availability at inference is verified before the feature is used
rules.description: Each feature's availability at prediction time — existence, latency, and quality — is verified before the feature enters the model, rather than discovered after deployment.
rules.rationale: Verification after the model is built converts a design question into a rebuild. Doing it first costs a conversation; doing it last costs the model.
rules.remediation: For each feature, confirm the inference path can reach its source within the latency budget, and record the finding in the lineage record.
rules.evidenceExpected: A per-feature availability determination, and an attestation that the inference path was checked against it.
rules.$assuranceNote: Nothing automated establishes this. What a production inference path can reach is a fact about infrastructure, which the repository does not describe.

rules.title: A model requiring absent features is not deployed
rules.description: A model must not be deployed when a feature it requires will not exist, with acceptable latency and quality, at the moment a prediction is made.
rules.rationale: Such a model has looked excellent in evaluation precisely because it had the input production will not give it. The failure surfaces after deployment, in whatever form the serving code improvises when the value is missing.
rules.remediation: Remove the unavailable feature and retrain, or make the feature available on the inference path with an acceptable latency, and re-evaluate either way.
rules.evidenceExpected: An attestation that every required feature was confirmed reachable at inference, listing the features and how each was confirmed.
rules.$assuranceNote: Nothing automated establishes this. The check would have to compare the model's feature list against a production system the repository cannot see.

rules.title: Prior exposure of the evaluation data is stated
rules.description: Where a pretrained artifact or a public benchmark takes part in evaluation, the record states what is known about the evaluation data's prior exposure, and does not describe the result as an unbiased estimate of generalisation unless exclusion is supported by evidence.
rules.rationale: Standard 8's other requirements reach only leakage the project's own pipeline creates. For a project fine-tuning a released checkpoint or reporting a public-benchmark number, the dominant leakage route is invisible to every one of them, because no transformation in the project's pipeline touched it. Kapoor & Narayanan (2023) catalogue eight leakage types across 294 affected papers in 17 fields.
rules.remediation: State which of three states holds: established overlap, an undetermined corpus, or exclusion supported by evidence such as a documented decontamination step or an evaluation set built after the artifact's cut-off. Report the number in any state; withhold the unbiased-estimate claim in the first two. Proving absence from an undisclosed corpus is not required.
rules.evidenceExpected: A recorded statement of prior exposure naming which of the three states holds, with the supporting evidence where exclusion is claimed, and the benchmark's reuse history where a public benchmark selected among candidates.
rules.$assuranceNote: Nothing automated establishes this. The training corpus of a released artifact is not in the repository, and for closed-weight artifacts is not published at all; a scan can see that a checkpoint is loaded and nothing about what it was trained on. Applicability itself is declared rather than detected — see the scope note in standards/08-leakage.md.
